slides: Okay, a quick summary before the advanced practice.
The methods from the last examples... in about three minutes.
Letters in the answers? Plug in a comfortable number that fits the figure.
So if p is obtuse, try a hundred and twenty. Then find q: fifty. Now put a hundred and twenty into every answer, and keep only the one that gives fifty.
And look for an exterior angle. It cuts the angle-sum equation short.
What if there are no lengths at all? Well, order the angles. The longest side is opposite the largest angle.
And you don't always need the full order. Only the largest angle.
An obtuse angle is always the largest. So the side opposite it is the longest.
Now, can't calculate it exactly? Then trap it between a minimum and a maximum.
Say AB is eight. The two other sides together are more than eight, so the perimeter is more than sixteen.
And if it's obtuse at C, then AB is the longest side. The other two are each less than eight, so the perimeter is less than twenty-four.
Now, the answers are in order? If a bigger answer fit, then every answer between it and the minimum would fit too. So only the smallest one above the minimum can be right.
"Not necessarily" questions. Go through the answers, and do the quick ones first.
A line that's two of the three, median, altitude, bisector, is a symmetry line. So the triangle is isosceles.
But a median alone can lean to one side. Sketch it, and you'll see the two sides come out different.
Not sure? Sketch a counterexample.
Shaded area? The main way is a shape you know, minus the white.
But complete the data first. For example, in an equilateral triangle, the altitude is also a median.
Or, split the shaded part into triangles with a known base and height. And an altitude outside still counts.
Two triangles with the same height? Then the area ratio is the base ratio.
So if DC is four times BD, the areas are one to four. Forty-five is five parts of nine... so nine and thirty-six.
A difference of two perimeters? Shared sides and equal sides cancel out. You don't need their lengths.
Out of time? Estimate. Root two is about one point four, root three about one point seven. And a negative length? Eliminate it.
A ratio? Check which way it goes. a is smaller than b, so a over b is less than one.
And you can always work back from the answers.
Okay, before you practice, ask yourself these questions.
And the traps: a ratio upside down, a perimeter that's equal to the minimum, and mixing up "could be" with "necessarily".
Good luck.
